title: What annual respirator training does OSHA require?
description: OSHA 1910.134(k) respirator training: seven knowledge elements, training before use, annual retraining, fit testing and voluntary use, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) respiratory protection standard, 29 CFR 1910.134(k), requires employers to train every employee who must wear a respirator before first use and to retrain at least annually. Each employee must be able to demonstrate knowledge of seven elements, from why the respirator is needed to recognizing medical symptoms that limit its use. Training must be understandable, provided at no cost, and repeated sooner when changes or knowledge gaps make earlier training obsolete.
keyTakeaways: Respirator training is annual: paragraph (k)(5) requires retraining at least annually, plus whenever workplace or respirator changes, knowledge gaps or other situations make it necessary.
The test is demonstrated knowledge. Paragraph (k)(1) requires each employee to be able to demonstrate knowledge of seven listed elements, not merely attend a session.
Training is separate from fit testing. Tight-fitting respirators also require a fit test before initial use and at least annually under paragraph (f)(2).
Employees who wear respirators voluntarily must receive the advisory information in Appendix D, which is mandatory for the employer to provide.
Respiratory protection (29 CFR 1910.134) ranked sixth in OSHA's preliminary list of most cited standards for fiscal year 2026.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Employers in general industry where respirators are necessary to protect employee health or are required by the employer, including manufacturing operations such as painting, welding, grinding, foundry work and chemical processing
Employees required to use respirators, and employees who use respirators voluntarily

sections.heading: When does the respirator training requirement apply?

blocks.text: The training requirement applies whenever respirators are necessary to protect employee health or the employer requires them. In those workplaces, paragraph (c)(1) of [29 CFR 1910.134](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.134) requires a written respiratory protection program with worksite-specific procedures, and two of its required elements are training: training in the respiratory hazards employees may be exposed to in routine and emergency situations (paragraph (c)(1)(vii)), and training in proper use, including putting on and removing respirators, limitations on their use, and maintenance (paragraph (c)(1)(viii)).

Paragraph (c)(4) requires the employer to provide respirators, training and medical evaluations at no cost to the employee. Paragraph (c)(3) requires a program administrator qualified by appropriate training or experience commensurate with the complexity of the program, which is itself a competence requirement for the person running it.

sections.heading: What must each respirator user be able to demonstrate?

blocks.text: Paragraph (k)(1) requires the employer to ensure each employee "can demonstrate knowledge of at least the following" seven elements:

items: Why the respirator is necessary and how improper fit, usage or maintenance can compromise its protective effect.
The limitations and capabilities of the respirator.
How to use the respirator effectively in emergency situations, including when it malfunctions.
How to inspect, put on and remove, use, and check the seals of the respirator.
The procedures for maintenance and storage.
How to recognize medical signs and symptoms that may limit or prevent effective use.
The general requirements of the standard.

blocks.text: Paragraph (k)(2) requires the training to be conducted in a manner that is understandable to the employee. Because the standard frames the outcome as a demonstration, the evidence should include an observed seal check and donning and doffing, not just a signed attendance sheet. The introductory text of paragraph (k) describes the training as needing to be "comprehensive, understandable, and recur annually, and more often if necessary."

sections.heading: When must respirator training and retraining happen?

blocks.text: Initial training must come before the employee is required to use a respirator in the workplace (paragraph (k)(3)). Retraining is required annually and earlier in three situations listed in paragraph (k)(5):

items: Changes in the workplace or the type of respirator render previous training obsolete.
Inadequacies in the employee's knowledge or use of the respirator indicate the employee has not retained the requisite understanding or skill.
Any other situation arises in which retraining appears necessary to ensure safe respirator use.

blocks.text: Paragraph (k)(4) gives one concession for new hires. If the employer can show a new employee received training within the last 12 months covering all seven elements, and the employee can demonstrate that knowledge, the employer need not repeat the training at hire. The previous training must still be renewed no later than 12 months from its original date, so the annual clock runs from the earlier training, not the hire date.

sections.heading: How do fit testing and medical evaluation relate to training?

blocks.text: Fit testing and medical evaluation are separate prerequisites that run alongside training. Under paragraph (f)(2), an employee using a tight-fitting facepiece respirator must be fit tested before initial use, whenever a different facepiece size, style, model or make is used, and at least annually thereafter. Paragraph (f)(3) adds a fit test when changes in the employee's physical condition, such as facial scarring, dental changes or an obvious change in body weight, could affect fit.

Records differ for each element. Under paragraph (m)(2), the fit test record must include the employee's name or identification, the type of fit test, the make, model, style and size of respirator tested, the date, and the result, and must be retained until the next fit test. Medical evaluation records follow 29 CFR 1910.1020 under paragraph (m)(1). Paragraph (m) does not prescribe a separate training record, but the written program, which must be retained under (m)(3), should describe how training is delivered and verified.

sections.heading: What training is required for voluntary respirator use?

blocks.text: Voluntary users must receive the advisory information in Appendix D. Under paragraph (c)(2)(i), if an employer permits voluntary respirator use, it must provide the information in Appendix D, titled "Information for Employees Using Respirators When Not Required Under the Standard", and paragraph (k)(6) allows it to be given in any written or oral format. Paragraph (o) makes Appendix D mandatory.

Voluntary users of filtering facepieces (dust masks) are excluded from the written program under the exception in paragraph (c)(2)(ii), but still receive Appendix D. Other voluntary users must be covered by the program elements needed to make sure they are medically able to use the respirator and that it is cleaned, stored and maintained properly.

sections.heading: What evidence shows a respirator training program is compliant?

blocks.text: An auditor will look for a link between each respirator user, their annual training, their fit test and their medical clearance. The table below maps each obligation to the person it applies to, its cycle and the evidence expected.

sections.heading: How is respirator training enforced, and how should it be built?

blocks.text: OSHA enforces the standard through inspections, and it is among the most cited. OSHA's [preliminary top 10 for fiscal year 2026](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) ranks respiratory protection in general industry sixth across all industries. Federal maximum penalties are published on [OSHA's penalties page](https://www.osha.gov/penalties).

Build the program around respirator type and hazard, because a change in either is a retraining trigger. Keep training, fit test and medical clearance dates on one record per employee so the annual cycles do not drift apart. Guidance on scheduling recurring cycles is in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles), and the chemical hazard content that respirator training should reference sits in [OSHA hazard communication training](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements). For an overview of OSHA duties across standards, see [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats the seven elements in paragraph (k)(1) as distinct assessment points, so annual retraining can show which elements each employee demonstrated and how. Changes to respirator models or hazards are recorded as change events that identify the employees whose earlier training may now be obsolete.

faqs.q: Is respirator training required every year?
faqs.a: Yes. Paragraph (k)(5) requires retraining annually for employees required to use respirators, and sooner when workplace or respirator changes, knowledge gaps or other situations make it necessary. Fit testing for tight-fitting respirators has its own separate annual requirement under paragraph (f)(2).

faqs.q: Can respirator training be delivered online?
faqs.a: Formal content can be delivered online, but the standard requires each employee to demonstrate knowledge, including how to inspect, put on, remove and seal check the respirator. Most employers add a hands-on demonstration to meet that element, and the training must be understandable to the employee.

faqs.q: Does a dust mask worn voluntarily require training?
faqs.a: The employer must give voluntary users the advisory information in Appendix D. Employees whose only respirator use is voluntary use of filtering facepieces are excluded from the written program, so the full training in paragraph (k)(1) is not required for them.

The employer. Paragraph (c)(4) requires respirators, training and medical evaluations to be provided at no cost to the employee. Scheduling training during paid working time is the simplest way to show that employees bore no cost for the annual cycle.
